Old New ttr-server-proto server-proto ttr-fuzzy-core lex-matcher-core ttr-text text ttr-meta-client meta-client ttr-llm-client llm-client ttr-transfer-core transfer-core

The toolchain keeps its prefix

If you consume the MCP doors: nothing.

If you deploy the Helm charts: the per-component chart names and image repositories moved, so a GitOps repository pinning chartPath or image.repository needs one editing pass:

# after

docs.title: OIDC and Keycloak
docs.text:
How-to. Wire your identity provider, and the verification duty that stays yours.

Tatrman decides what each user may see. It can only do that if the real user's identity reaches the validator on every call — and if the token carrying that identity is verified before it does. Agents forward the token (that is their job); verifying it is yours.

docs.title: Wire your IdP
docs.text:
Set the auth.* keys (see The values contract):

auth:
  issuerUrl: https://idp.example.com/realms/yourrealm
  audience: tatrman
  jwksUri: https://idp.example.com/realms/yourrealm/protocol/openid-connect/certs
  realm: yourrealm
  verification: ingress        # or in-door

The reference IdP is Keycloak; any OIDC provider works. The platform reads exactly two facts from a token — the user id (preferred_username, falling back to sub) and the roles (realm_access.roles). If your IdP names these differently, map them to those two claims in your IdP configuration. The platform does not reshape claims, and neither should your agents.

docs.title: The verification duty — do not skip it
docs.text:
Deployments MUST verify the bearer token before pipeline entry. The mechanism is free:

  • verification: ingress — terminate and verify at the ingress/sidecar, and let the door extract already-trusted claims. (The live pilot does this.)
  • verification: in-door — the door verifies the token itself.

Either is conforming. What is not conforming is skipping verification and trusting whatever identity arrives — that is an unguarded system that looks guarded. If you take one thing from this page: an operator who skips token verification has removed the platform's entire governance guarantee while leaving every green checkmark in place.

docs.title: Keep the shortcuts off
docs.text: auth.trustedNetworkShortcuts (the X-User-Id header, the user_id argument) defaults off and should stay off unless you own the entire call path and know exactly what you are trusting. They are outside the identity contract, and any conformant agent ignores them anyway. When a real bearer token resolves, they are ignored regardless.

docs.title: For the quickstart only
docs.text: devIdp.* gives you a throwaway Keycloak with a seeded realm and a demo/demo user so a first run works without an IdP. Turn it off and wire the auth.* keys above before anyone real uses the system.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
• A call with no token is refused (missing_user_identity) — good.
  • A service-account token with no user claim is refused — agents never call as themselves.
  • The same governed question asked by two different users returns different pipelineWarnings — the per-user filters are being applied. That difference is the proof your identity wiring works.

docs.title: Policy in git
docs.text:
How-to. Writing, reviewing and shipping policy the same way you ship the model.

Tatrman's access policy — who may see which rows, which columns are masked, which roles a question requires — is not clicked into a console. It lives in an open validator store: text, versioned in git, reviewed in a pull request, and shipped like any other change. This is deliberate. Policy that lives in a UI has no history, no review, and no diff; policy that lives in git has all three.

docs.title: The shape of it
docs.text:
• Policy is text in a store (HOCON), versioned beside the model it governs.
  • Robots write through git. The tools that propose changes — ttr import-schema, a harvest connector — never mutate live configuration. They open a pull request. A human reviews and merges; the merge is the deployment. Nothing changes under you without a diff you approved.
  • The validator reads the store. At request time the validator applies the policy from the store to the per-user identity the door forwarded, and records what it did in pipelineWarnings. Change the policy in git, ship it, and the next request reflects it.

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text:
1. Edit the policy in the store, in a branch — the same repository discipline you use for the model.
  2. Review it in a pull request. Because it is text, a reviewer sees exactly what changed: a new row-level filter, a column newly masked, a role requirement added or removed.
  3. Ship by merging. The running system picks up the merged policy; the change is auditable forever because it is a commit.

docs.title: Why this matters to you as an operator
docs.text:
• Every access decision is auditable after the fact. When someone asks "why could they see that?" six months later, the answer is a commit — the policy that was in force, who approved it, and when.
  • Least privilege is reviewable, not assumed. A widening of access is a diff a second person signed off on, not a checkbox nobody remembers ticking.
  • The same review muscle covers model and policy. You already review the model in git; policy rides the same rails, so there is no second, weaker change-management path around your governance.

Pair this with OIDC and Keycloak: identity says who is asking, policy in git says what they may see, and pipelineWarnings on every answer says what was applied.

docs.title: Deploy the Studio Viewer
docs.text:
How-to. Run the read-only model viewer next to a Veles catalog.

The Studio Viewer is the open, read-only view of a Tatrman model. In catalog mode it reads the model a Veles instance serves, through Veles' JSON read API, and draws the ER and DB graphs, with an inspector and search on top. It never writes anything to the server: there is no edit, and no call outside the read routes listed below. A picture you arrange — which cards, where — is a layout, and it leaves the viewer only as a download (see Layouts); git is how it is shared.

It ships as one container image: a static bundle behind nginx.

ghcr.io/collite/ttr-viewer:<version>
Process nginx, unprivileged (uid 101) Port 8080 (VIEWER_PORT) Health GET /healthz → 200 ok, outside the base path Platforms linux/amd64, linux/arm64 Writes /tmp only. Read-only root filesystem works; mount an emptyDir at /tmp.

docs.title: Configure it
docs.text:
Everything is environment, read once when the container starts. Nothing is baked in at build time, and nothing depends on a query parameter. The entrypoint refuses a value it cannot use (exit code 64, with the reason on stderr) instead of starting with a guess.

Variable Default Meaning VIEWER_BASE_PATH / The path prefix the viewer is served under, e.g. /models/. The bare prefix redirects to its slash form, and nothing outside the prefix is served. VIEWER_CATALOG_URL <base>veles The catalog the browser reads: a same-origin path (/models/veles), an http(s):// origin, or a ws(s):// origin (the platform transport). none means no catalog: the viewer opens on its local landing card. VIEWER_CATALOG_UPSTREAM unset Veles' HTTP origin, e.g. http://veles.ttr-server.svc:7260. When set, nginx proxies <base>veles/ to it, read routes only (see below). When unset, <base>veles/ answers 503 with a JSON error. VIEWER_DEFAULT_LANG unset The language for model labels and descriptions when neither the URL nor the user picked one. Unset means the browser's language, then en. VIEWER_LANGUAGES unset Extra languages the language picker offers, comma-separated (en,cs). The model's own labels add theirs. VIEWER_LAYOUT_FORMAT yaml The format Save as… offers first: yaml or ttr. Once a user picks one, their choice wins in that browser. VIEWER_PORT 8080 The listen port.

The entrypoint renders these into two files the app reads:

  • <base>config.json — { "basePath", "veles", "lang", "languages", "layoutFormat" }, fetched once before the first render.
  • <base>index.html — with <base href="<base>">, so every asset URL resolves under the prefix.

docs.title: URLs
docs.text:
The viewer keeps its state in the address bar, under the base path:

https://apps.example.com/models/w/<workspace>/s/<schema>      e.g. …/models/w/veles/s/er

A reload or a bookmark of that URL opens the same graph. Only the base path the image was given is served; deep links below it all get the app.

For local use, ?veles=<catalog> still selects a catalog explicitly and wins over the configured one, e.g. http://localhost:5173/?veles=http://localhost:7260 against the dev server. The address bar keeps it on every rewrite, so reloads keep the catalog.

docs.title: Labels and language
docs.text:
The viewer shows the model the way its authors labelled it, not by identifier. An entity's card reads its displayLabel in the viewer's language, Product for the Hartland model's item, and falls back to the identifier when no label exists in that language. Attributes become rows of their entity's card (choose With types under Detail to see them), and relations become the edges between cards, with their cardinality.

Select a card to open the inspector. It shows the label, the identifier and qualified name (item, er.entity.item), the plural label (Products), the description, and every attribute with its own description. A description in the viewer's language wins; failing that, the plain-form description, then English, then the first one the model has.

The language is chosen when the page loads, first match wins:

  1. ?lang=cs in the URL, which the address bar keeps;
  2. the user's own choice from the Language picker in the header (remembered in that browser);
  3. VIEWER_DEFAULT_LANG;
  4. the browser's language;
  5. en.

The picker offers the languages the model's labels carry, plus VIEWER_LANGUAGES. The viewer's own buttons and headings stay English.

Needs a Veles that serves the labels

The labels, descriptions and relation endpoints are fields of Veles' JSON read API from the release after 0.11.7 (Collite/ttr-server#185). Against an older Veles the viewer still works, but it shows identifiers, and relations appear as cards of their own instead of edges.

docs.title: Layouts: pick, place, save
docs.text:
A schema opens whole: every entity (or table) the catalog serves, laid out automatically. To draw a smaller picture, use the Objects panel on the left of the canvas — every card of the schema, grouped by package, each with a checkbox. Uncheck what you do not need; search narrows the list (label, identifier, qualified name, package), and All · None · Neighbours · Invert act on it. The first such change turns the tab into a new layout, er · untitled, marked * while it has unsaved changes.

  • Relations through hidden cards. When two shown cards are joined only through a card you hid, a dashed … edge connects them (… ×2 when there are several such cards). Click it: the inspector names the hidden card(s) and the two relations each joins, with Show to bring one back.
  • Right-click a card for Expand (+n) (add its direct neighbours), Expand all levels… (everything reachable through hidden cards, after a confirmation that says how many), Hide, Hide others (keep the card and its visible neighbours) and Inspect. Shift-click selects several cards; the menu then acts on all of them. Each row of the panel offers Expand and Hide on hover too.
  • Drag cards where you want them. A card you check later is placed beside its nearest visible neighbour, and nothing you placed moves. Re-layout arranges everything shown automatically.
  • Save as… downloads the layout as YAML (<name>.yaml) or TTR (<name>.ttrg), showing the exact text first. The name follows the graph-name rule: letters, digits and underscore, not starting with a digit. The TTR form does not carry the notation (skin); the dialog says so.
  • Open layout… (or drop a file on the canvas) reads a .yaml, or a .ttrg together with its .ttrl sidecar, and opens it in a new tab. Objects can be named in any of the forms the layout format accepts, bare names included; a name the model does not have is listed under Missing in the panel, kept until you remove it.

The truth chip above the canvas says where the picture lives: layout: file · unsaved, layout: file · sales.yaml, layout: catalog · sales. Nothing of this is stored on the server; leaving the page with unsaved changes asks first. A downloaded layout file is shared the way the model is: commit it next to the model, and a catalog that serves layouts lists it in the spine as er · <name> for everyone, with a link of its own. A layout opened from your disk has no shareable link.

docs.title: The catalog proxy: read routes only
docs.text:
The viewer's catalog calls are same-origin fetches to <base>veles/…. With VIEWER_CATALOG_UPSTREAM set, the image's nginx forwards exactly these, GET only:

Route Used for /model/index packages, schemas, counts, model version /model/graph a schema's graph /model/object one object's detail /model/search search /model/layouts the layouts committed next to the model (the spine's er · <name> entries) /model/layout one layout, resolved against the model /status polled for a new model version

Everything else under <base>veles/ is a 404 at the viewer, in particular POST /refresh, /admin/*, /model/export, /model/export/dot and /metrics; a read route asked with anything but GET is a 403. The matches are exact, so /model/export cannot ride in on a /model/ prefix.

docs.title: Layouts the catalog serves
docs.text:
A layout file committed under the model root — a .ttrg the viewer's Save as… wrote, with its .ttrl sidecar when there is one — is served to every viewer of that model: Veles reads the layout files with each model load, resolves their cards against that model and answers /model/layouts and /model/layout?name= from them. The model's own files load as before; a layout file is never read as model. A layout file that cannot be read (not UTF-8 text) or does not parse is left out and listed in /status under issues (layout layouts/sales.ttrg: …; a problem in the sidecar names the .ttrl and its line). When two files declare the same layout name, neither is served — each is listed, naming the other — so which picture a viewer gets never depends on file order. The model is served regardless. The sidecar is read as the viewer reads it: a property a layout does not use (viewport, …) is skipped. There is no write route: committing the file to the model's repository is how a layout is published.

The proxy also drops the Cookie header. The session cookie belongs to the edge (next section), and Veles reads none. Identity headers an authenticating proxy adds (X-Forwarded-User, X-Auth-Request-*) pass through unchanged.

Keep Veles itself off the edge

Veles' HTTP port also serves /refresh (unauthenticated, cluster-internal by design) and the model export. Expose the viewer, never Veles. Restrict Veles' HTTP port to in-cluster callers with a NetworkPolicy, so that the viewer is the only browser-facing path to it.

docs.title: The auth seam: a cookie-session edge
docs.text:
The viewer cannot attach a bearer token. It is a static app with no OIDC client of its own, and its catalog calls are same-origin fetch with credentials: 'include': the browser sends its cookies and nothing else. So the supported setup is an authenticating proxy at the edge that logs the browser in and keeps a cookie session, e.g. oauth2-proxy in front of the viewer, or your ingress controller's external-auth feature pointed at one:

browser ──cookie──▶ edge (OIDC login, session cookie) ──▶ ttr-viewer :8080 ──read routes──▶ Veles :7260
  • The edge protects everything under the base path, <base>veles/… included. An unauthenticated request is redirected to the IdP; the session cookie then carries every request after it.
  • The viewer adds no authorization of its own. Whoever passes the edge reads the whole catalog the upstream Veles serves. Scope the catalog by what that Veles loads, not by the viewer.
  • /healthz sits outside the base path, so probes need no session.

docs.title: Reference: Kubernetes with ingress-nginx and oauth2-proxy
docs.text:
The viewer and its catalog proxy run in one pod. oauth2-proxy (deployed separately, with your IdP's client) guards the ingress:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ttr-viewer
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: ttr-viewer }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: ttr-viewer }
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 101
      containers:
        - name: viewer
          image: ghcr.io/collite/ttr-viewer:<version>
          env:
            - { name: VIEWER_BASE_PATH, value: /models/ }
            - { name: VIEWER_CATALOG_UPSTREAM, value: http://veles.ttr-server.svc.cluster.local:7260 }
            - { name: VIEWER_DEFAULT_LANG, value: en }
          ports:
            - { name: http, containerPort: 8080 }
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: http } }
          livenessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: http } }
          securityContext:
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            capabilities: { drop: [ALL] }
          volumeMounts:
            - { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp }
      volumes:
        - name: tmp
          emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: ttr-viewer
spec:
  selector: { app: ttr-viewer }
  ports:
    - { name: http, port: 80, targetPort: http }
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: ttr-viewer
  annotations:
    # every request under /models/ needs an oauth2-proxy session (cookie); none → IdP login
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-url: "https://$host/oauth2/auth"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-signin: "https://$host/oauth2/start?rd=$escaped_request_uri"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: apps.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /models/
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: { name: ttr-viewer, port: { name: http } }

nginx resolves VIEWER_CATALOG_UPSTREAM's host name when it starts. A Kubernetes Service name resolves even before its pods are ready, but a name that does not exist at all stops the container.

docs.title: Reference: your own edge routes the catalog
docs.text:
If your edge already routes <base>veles/ to Veles, leave VIEWER_CATALOG_UPSTREAM unset. The edge then owns the allow-list. This is the nginx equivalent of the image's own proxy, for a viewer at /:

location = /veles/model/index   { limit_except GET { deny all; } proxy_pass http://veles:7260/model/index;   proxy_set_header Cookie ""; }
location = /veles/model/graph   { limit_except GET { deny all; } proxy_pass http://veles:7260/model/graph;   proxy_set_header Cookie ""; }
location = /veles/model/object  { limit_except GET { deny all; } proxy_pass http://veles:7260/model/object;  proxy_set_header Cookie ""; }
location = /veles/model/search  { limit_except GET { deny all; } proxy_pass http://veles:7260/model/search;  proxy_set_header Cookie ""; }
location = /veles/model/layouts { limit_except GET { deny all; } proxy_pass http://veles:7260/model/layouts; proxy_set_header Cookie ""; }
location = /veles/model/layout  { limit_except GET { deny all; } proxy_pass http://veles:7260/model/layout;  proxy_set_header Cookie ""; }
location = /veles/status        { limit_except GET { deny all; } proxy_pass http://veles:7260/status;        proxy_set_header Cookie ""; }
location ^~ /veles/             { return 404; }

docs.title: Try it locally: the Hartland demo model
docs.text:
Veles serves a model from a directory with its filesystem source. The public demo model (Collite/ttr-demo, under model/) works as is:

git clone https://github.com/Collite/ttr-demo.git
docker network create ttr-viewer-demo

docker run -d --name veles --network ttr-viewer-demo \
  -v "$PWD/ttr-demo/model:/model:ro" \
  -e METADATA_TTR_ROOT=/model \
  -e JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS='-Dmetadata.sources.fixture.enabled=true -Dmetadata.sources.github-model.enabled=false' \
  ghcr.io/collite/veles:<version>

docker run -d --name viewer --network ttr-viewer-demo -p 8080:8080 \
  -e VIEWER_CATALOG_UPSTREAM=http://veles:7260 \
  ghcr.io/collite/ttr-viewer:<version>

Open http://localhost:8080/ and choose er in the catalog: the Hartland ER graph opens, with cards that read Product, Store, Customer Address, and so on. Open http://localhost:8080/?lang=cs and the same cards read Produkt, Prodejna, Adresa zákazníka. Add -e VIEWER_BASE_PATH=/models/ to the viewer to serve it under http://localhost:8080/models/ instead.

Use a Veles that serves the labels (see Labels and language). With 0.11.7 the graph shows identifiers.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/healthz                       # ok
curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/config.json                   # the rendered runtime config
curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/veles/model/index             # the catalog, through the proxy
curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/veles/model/layouts           # the layouts the catalog serves
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST http://localhost:8080/veles/refresh   # 404: not a read route

docs.title: Upgrade and versioning
docs.text:
Reference. What the product version promises you.

You upgrade Tatrman the way you upgrade any Helm release — but the number you are upgrading to carries a promise, and knowing it is the difference between a routine bump and a careful migration.

docs.title: The product version
docs.text:
The chart's appVersion is the product version. It is the one number that tells you what changed for you as an operator and as a consumer:

  • Within a major version, the wire surface is additive. The MCP tools your agents call, and the result envelope they read, only grow — new optional inputs, new output fields. A conformant agent keeps working across every minor and patch bump without you touching it (this is the compatibility rule, from the consumer's seat).
  • A breaking wire change ships as a new major, and as a new :v2 capability alongside the :v1 it replaces — never in place. You migrate deliberately; nothing is pulled out from under a running agent within a major.
  • Deprecated is not removed within a major. A capability marked deprecated keeps answering; the window is documented in the capability manifest.

docs.title: Image tags follow the product
docs.text: Service images resolve by the precedence image.tag → global.image.tag → appVersion. Pin global.image.tag to the product version you intend to run and leave per-service tags unset for a uniform, reproducible install. An upgrade is then a single value change plus helm upgrade.

docs.title: The documentation is versioned too
docs.text: The docs site is published with mike: before 1.0.0 it serves a rolling latest; from 1.0.0 onward each product version gets its own labelled snapshot. Read the docs for the version you run, not the tip — the snapshot for your appVersion describes the surface you actually have.

docs.title: Before you upgrade
docs.text:
• Read the release notes for the target appVersion — a minor/patch is additive; a new major names its :v2 capabilities and deprecations.
  • Bump global.image.tag and helm upgrade.
  • Confirm every pod returns to Ready and the front door's /ready is green.
  • Re-run your agent's conformance check — green means the surface your agent depends on survived the upgrade.

docs.title: The values contract
docs.text:
Reference. Every key the umbrella chart honours, what it does, and what happens if you leave it at its default. This page is the operator's projection of the chart's documented values contract; the canonical contract ships with the chart and is the source of truth — if a key is not in it, do not guess what it does.

The umbrella chart installs the whole product from one release. You configure it with values; this page is the contract for those values, so nothing is folklore reconstructed from defaults.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
• global.image.tag — the product image tag applied across services. Precedence for any one service is image.tag (per-service override) → global.image.tag → the chart's appVersion. Leave per-service tags unset and pin global.image.tag for a uniform install.
  • Enable toggles — each service has an <name>.enabled flag. The chart ships a sensible default set; turn a service off and its workload is not rendered. The value key is not always the image or directory name — the contract's key↔image map is the authority.

docs.title: Identity and OIDC (the keys you must get right)
docs.text:
Governance is per-user, so identity configuration is not optional. Under auth:

  • auth.issuerUrl — your OIDC issuer.
  • auth.audience — the expected token audience.
  • auth.jwksUri — where the doors fetch signing keys.
  • auth.realm — the realm (Keycloak-shaped).
  • auth.verification — ingress or in-door: where the bearer token is verified before pipeline entry. The mechanism is yours to choose; that verification happens at all is not — see OIDC and Keycloak.
  • auth.trustedNetworkShortcuts — default off. The X-User-Id / user_id edge shortcuts are outside the MCP identity contract; enabling them is your authority alone, and they are ignored whenever a real bearer token resolves.

The claim conventions (user id from preferred_username→sub, roles from realm_access.roles) are fixed by the identity contract and are not configurable — only the mapping from your IdP to those two facts is.

docs.title: Dev Keycloak — quickstart only
docs.text: devIdp.* stands up a throwaway Keycloak that seeds a realm, a tatrman-agent public client, and a demo/demo user. It exists so a stranger can complete the quickstart without wiring an IdP first. It is not for production — bring your own IdP and set the auth.* keys above.

docs.title: Understanding-layer and per-service config
docs.text:
• nlp.backends.*, geo.*, resolver.* — configuration for the understanding layer (grounding, resolution, fuzzy). UFAL/NC-licensed NLP backends are opt-in and off by default.
  • Per-service passthrough — each service exposes its own values under its key for resource requests, replicas and service-specific settings.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
The chart's appVersion is the product version — the promise you get about compatibility across an upgrade. See Upgrade and versioning for what it commits to (RO-24).

For the full key-by-key list, resource defaults and the value-key↔image map, read the canonical contract linked at the top of this page — this projection covers the keys an operator sets, not every internal default.
